set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which statement correctly describes the cell population of the epidermis?
opts: Keratinocytes (about 90 percent), melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells
Correct. The epidermis holds keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, and keratinocytes, which produce keratin, make up about 90 percent of it.
Fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes and mast cells, with fibroblasts predominating
Fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes and mast cells are cells of the dermis; the epidermis holds keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells.
Melanocytes, Merkel cells, fibroblasts and histiocytes, with melanocytes predominating
Fibroblasts and histiocytes are dermal cells, and melanocytes are a minority; keratinocytes make up about 90 percent of the epidermis.
Keratinocytes and melanocytes only, in roughly equal proportion
The epidermis has four cell types, adding Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, and keratinocytes far outnumber melanocytes at about 90 percent.

set1.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: A nodule is greater than 5 millimeters. What tissue does it arise from?
opts: Superficial epidermis only, with no dermal involvement
A nodule is not confined to the epidermis; it is a dermal-based lesion of dense collagen bundles that extends into subcutaneous tissue.
Fluid accumulating between epidermis and dermis
Fluid collecting between a separated epidermis and dermis describes a bulla; a nodule is solid, built of dense dermal collagen bundles and subcutaneous tissue.
Dilated superficial dermal capillaries with no inflammatory infiltration at all
Dilated superficial dermal capillaries without inflammatory infiltrate define telangiectasia; a nodule is a solid lesion of dense dermal collagen bundles.
Dermal-based tissue with dense collagen bundles, extending into subcutaneous tissue
Correct. A nodule is an elevated, solid lesion over 5 millimeters: a dermal-based lesion of dense collagen bundles extending into subcutaneous tissue.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which description of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is accurate?
opts: The skin alone, with no systemic involvement whatsoever, at any age at all
Henoch-Schonlein purpura is not limited to the skin; this immunoglobulin A vasculitis involves the skin, joints, kidneys and intestines.
Skin, joints, kidneys and intestines, commonly in children aged 3 to 10 years
Correct — an immunoglobulin A vasculitis, which is why it is not confined to the skin.
Skin and lungs only, commonly in older adults
The lungs are not among the organs involved, and it is common in children aged 3 to 10 rather than older adults; skin, joints, kidneys and intestines are affected.
Skin and liver, commonly in neonates
The liver is not among the organs involved and neonates are not the usual group; it involves skin, joints, kidneys and intestines in children aged 3 to 10.

set1.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: How do hypertrophic scars and keloids depart from normal healing?
opts: Keratinocyte division slows and elastin degrades, thinning the tissue
Slowed keratinocyte division and elastin degradation describe atrophy, which thins the skin; keloids come from a prolonged proliferative phase and excess collagen.

The inflammatory phase never resolves, so granulation tissue never forms at all and the wound remains open indefinitely without ever progressing to the proliferative or remodeling phases that normally follow
Hypertrophic scars and keloids do progress through healing; fibroblast dysregulation prolongs the proliferative phase rather than preventing it.
Type I collagen is replaced by weaker type III in basket-weave orientation
Remodeling normally replaces type III collagen with stronger type I; in keloids the defect is an imbalance of collagen deposition and degradation during remodeling.
Fibroblast dysregulation prolongs the proliferative phase and unbalances remodeling, so collagen bundles grow haphazardly beyond the original wound
Correct. Two phases go wrong: proliferation is prolonged, and collagen deposition and degradation become imbalanced during remodeling. Exceeding the original wound margin is the defining outcome.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which description of leukonychia is accurate?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed
Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed produces Terry's nails, opaque except for a dark band at the tip; leukonychia is incomplete keratinization.
Increased capillary density with release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the nail bed tissue itself
Increased capillary density with vascular endothelial growth factor release is the finding in clubbing; leukonychia comes from incomplete keratinization.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed, usually from harmless nail bed damage

Correct. Leukonychia, or Mee's lines, shows white streaks or spots from temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed, usually from harmless nail bed damage, though it is also seen with heavy metal poisoning.
A halt of keratin production, associated with illness and malnourishment
A halt of keratin production causes Beau's lines, which are transverse grooves; leukonychia shows white streaks or spots from incomplete keratinization.

set1.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: Which description of the inflammatory phase of wound healing is accurate?
opts: Days 1 to 3: type I collagen is laid down in basket-weave orientation
Collagen replacement happens in remodeling, days 21 to one year, when type I collagen lies in parallel bundles; days 1 to 3 bring the fibrin plug and clearance.
Days 1 to 3: a fibrin hemostatic plug forms, neutrophils and macrophages remove dead tissue, and growth factors are secreted
Correct. The phase both cleans the wound and issues the signal, through secreted growth factors and cytokines, that starts proliferation.
Days 4 to 21: granulation tissue forms, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells that rebuild the wound bed from below over three weeks
Granulation tissue forming over days 4 to 21 is the proliferative phase; the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 3, forms a fibrin plug and clears dead tissue.
Days 21 to one year: type III collagen is replaced by type I
Replacement of type III collagen by type I is the remodeling phase, days 21 to one year; the inflammatory phase spans days 1 to 3.

set1.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: What distinguishes a vesicle from a bulla?
opts: A vesicle is up to 5 millimeters, with fluid within or beneath the epidermis; a bulla is larger and separates epidermis from dermis

Correct. A vesicle holds fluid containing inflammatory cells within or directly beneath the epidermis; a bulla, greater than 5 millimeters, involves separation of epidermis from dermis. The bulla represents a deeper plane of cleavage, not merely a bigger blister.

A vesicle is greater than 5 millimeters and a bulla is up to 5 millimeters in diameter, and the two share an identical mechanism of fluid accumulation entirely within the epidermis rather than beneath it
The sizes are reversed: a vesicle is up to 5 millimeters and a bulla is larger, and a bulla forms by separation of the epidermis from the dermis.
A vesicle is solid and a bulla is fluid-filled
Both are fluid-filled lesions; a vesicle collects fluid within or beneath the epidermis, and a bulla forms where the epidermis separates from the dermis.
A vesicle contains purulent material and a bulla contains serous fluid
Purulent material of leukocytes and debris defines a pustule; vesicle fluid contains inflammatory cells, and bulla fluid collects between epidermis and dermis.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Eczematous dermatitis results from which type of inflammatory reaction?
opts: T cell-mediated
Correct. Eczematous dermatitis typically results from T cell-mediated inflammatory reactions, with insufficient filaggrin compromising the epidermal barrier.
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation alone
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing histamine produces the wheals of urticaria; eczema is a T cell-mediated inflammatory reaction.
Neutrophil-driven suppurative inflammation
Purulent, leukocyte-rich material fills a pustule; eczema results from T cell-mediated inflammatory reactions rather than suppurative inflammation.
Complement-mediated vessel destruction
Vessel destruction is not the mechanism of eczema; eczematous dermatitis results from T cell-mediated inflammation plus a filaggrin-deficient barrier.

set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which dermal cell mediates immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation?
opts: The mast cell
Correct, and its degranulation is the mechanism behind both the wheal and urticaria.
The fibroblast
Fibroblasts produce the collagen that gives the dermis tensile strength; the mast cell is the dermal cell behind immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation.
The melanocyte
Melanocytes are pigment cells of the epidermal basal layer; the mast cell is the dermal cell that mediates immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation.
The keratinocyte
Keratinocytes make up about 90 percent of the epidermis and produce keratin; mast cells mediate immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation in the dermis.

set1.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: How are dermatofibroma and lipoma characterized in the tissue?
opts: Dermatofibroma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes; lipoma is a fibrous tissue overgrowth within the dermis
This swaps the two: dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis, and lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes.
Both are malignant proliferations of keratinocytes
Both are benign, and neither is keratinocyte-derived: dermatofibroma is fibrous tissue in the dermis and lipoma is encapsulated adipocytes.
Dermatofibroma is keratin-filled and lipoma is fluid-filled
Keratin filling describes an epidermal inclusion cyst from a hair follicle; dermatofibroma is fibrous tissue and lipoma is a capsule of adipocytes.
Dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis; lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes
Correct. Dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis, and lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes.

set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What are the two connective tissue layers of the dermis?
opts: Basale and spinosum
The stratum basale and stratum spinosum are epidermal layers; the dermis has a thin superficial papillary layer and a dense deeper reticular layer.
Corneum and lucidum
The stratum corneum and stratum lucidum are outer epidermal layers; the dermis consists of the papillary and reticular connective tissue layers.
The papillary and the subcutaneous, being the superficial and the deepest layers
The subcutaneous layer, or hypodermis, is the third layer of skin rather than dermis; the deeper dermal layer is the dense reticular layer.
Papillary, the thin superficial layer, and reticular, the dense deeper layer
Correct. The dermis consists of two connective tissue layers: the thin superficial papillary layer and the dense deeper reticular layer.

set1.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What defines a secondary skin lesion?
opts: Any lesion that arises from malignant rather than from benign underlying disease processes
Malignancy plays no part in the definition; a secondary lesion is a primary lesion modified by infection, trauma or other factors.
A modification or change of a primary lesion caused by infection, trauma or other factors
Correct, which is why a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble what it came from.
Any lesion appearing on a second body site after the first
Location is not the criterion; a secondary lesion is a primary lesion that has been modified or changed by infection, trauma or other factors.
Any lesion that is palpable rather than flat
Palpability separates papules and nodules from flat macules within the primary group; a secondary lesion is a modified primary lesion.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which description of petechiae is accurate?
opts: Mast cell histamine release with plasma leakage, up to 5 millimeters
Histamine release from mast cells with plasma leaking into the dermis produces a wheal; petechiae are pinpoint deposits of blood from capillary rupture.
Minor bleeding into the dermis, such as from capillary rupture, 1 to 2 millimeters or less
Correct. Petechiae are non-blanchable pinpoint deposits of blood in the dermis, 1 to 2 millimeters or less, from minor bleeding such as capillary rupture, infection, thrombocytopenia or vasculitis.
Permanent dilatation of the superficial dermal vessels, measuring 1 to 2 millimeters across the surface of the skin
Permanent dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels is telangiectasia; petechiae are pinpoint deposits of blood from bleeding into the dermis.
Increased melanin production in the basal layer, up to 5 millimeters
Increased melanin production in the basal layer produces a hyperpigmented macule; petechiae are red or purple deposits of blood 1 to 2 millimeters or less.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which mechanism underlies basal cell carcinoma?
opts: The Hedgehog pathway, after ultraviolet-induced mutation of basal keratinocytes
Correct. Ultraviolet-induced mutation of basal keratinocytes overactivates Hedgehog signaling and drives tumor growth in this slow-growing, rarely metastasizing cancer.
The tp53 tumor suppressor pathway, acting in the differentiated keratinocytes of the epidermis
The tp53 tumor suppressor gene mutation belongs to squamous cell carcinoma; basal cell carcinoma overactivates the Hedgehog signaling pathway in basal keratinocytes.
Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, in immature keratinocytes
Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 is proposed for benign seborrheic keratosis; basal cell carcinoma overactivates Hedgehog signaling.
Uninhibited melanocyte growth at the dermal-epidermal junction
Uninhibited melanocyte growth at the dermal-epidermal junction is melanoma; basal cell carcinoma arises from mutated basal keratinocytes via Hedgehog signaling.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which description of actinic keratosis is accurate?
opts: Benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes, carrying a higher risk for basal cell carcinoma of the head and neck region in later life especially
Benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes is seborrheic keratosis; actinic keratosis is dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation raising squamous cell carcinoma risk.
Human papillomavirus infection of basal cells, carrying higher risk for melanoma
Human papillomavirus invading basal cells produces verrucae vulgaris; actinic keratosis stems from cumulative ultraviolet damage and raises squamous cell carcinoma risk.
Autoimmune T cell infiltration, carrying higher risk for lymphoma
Autoimmune T cell infiltration fits psoriasis, not actinic keratosis, which is ultraviolet-driven dysplasia carrying a higher risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
Cumulative ultraviolet damage causing intraepidermal proliferation of dysplastic keratinocytes, raising squamous cell carcinoma risk
Correct. Actinic keratosis is the most common precancer, arising on skin damaged by chronic ultraviolet exposure, and it carries a higher risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: How do petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses differ?
opts: By size — petechiae 1 to 2 millimeters or less, purpura 3 to 10 millimeters, ecchymoses greater than 10 millimeters — with similar underlying pathology
Correct. All three are bleeding into the dermis with similar underlying pathology, separated by size, from pinpoint petechiae to ecchymoses over 10 millimeters.
By mechanism — petechiae from capillary rupture, purpura from vessel dilatation, and ecchymoses from melanin deposition in the dermis rather than blood
The mechanism does not change between them: all three are non-blanchable deposits of blood in the dermis, and ecchymoses contain blood, not melanin.
By depth — petechiae epidermal, purpura dermal, ecchymoses subcutaneous
All three are deposits of blood in the dermis, not at different depths; they are separated by size, from pinpoint petechiae to ecchymoses over 10 millimeters.
By blanchability — petechiae blanch, purpura and ecchymoses do not
None of the three blanches: petechiae and purpura are non-blanchable deposits of blood in the dermis, and the distinction between them is size.

set1.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: What distinguishes a primary from a secondary skin lesion?
opts: A primary lesion is the one that appears first in time, and a secondary lesion is any lesion that appears later at a different site elsewhere on the body
Timing and body site do not define it; a secondary lesion is one modified over time, while a primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease.
A primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease and retains its original unmodified appearance; a secondary lesion has been modified over time
Correct, and a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble the lesion it came from.
A primary lesion is palpable and a secondary lesion is flat
Palpability separates papules, nodules and plaques from flat macules within the primary group; a secondary lesion is instead one modified over time.
A primary lesion is benign and a secondary lesion is malignant
Neither category implies malignancy; a primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease, while a secondary one has been modified over time.

set1.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: Which description of a fissure is accurate?
opts: A thickened plaque produced by chronic rubbing
A thickened plaque from chronic rubbing is lichenification; a fissure is a linear crack in the epidermis from dryness, lost elasticity and mechanical tension.
A dilated superficial vessel without inflammatory infiltrate
A dilated superficial vessel without infiltrate is telangiectasia; a fissure is a linear ulcer that cracks the epidermis under mechanical tension.
A linear ulcer cracking the epidermis, from lost elasticity, severe dryness and mechanical tension
Correct. A fissure is a linear ulcer cracking the epidermis where lost elasticity, severe dryness and mechanical tension act on a thickened stratum corneum.
A superficial loss of the epidermis that spares the dermal-epidermal junction and everything beneath it, so no collagen is ever destroyed in the process of healing
Superficial epidermal loss sparing the dermal-epidermal junction is an erosion; a fissure is a linear, crack-shaped ulcer in the epidermis.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which tinea subtype affects the nails?
opts: Tinea barbae, affecting nails and beard
Tinea barbae affects the beard area, not the nails; the nail infection is tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis.
Tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis
Correct. Corporis is trunk and limbs, pedis foot, cruris groin, capitis head, facialis face, manuum hand, barbae beard.
Tinea capitis, also called onychomycosis
Tinea capitis affects the head; onychomycosis is the other name for tinea unguium, the dermatophyte infection of the nails.
Tinea manuum, affecting the nails of the hand
Tinea manuum affects the hand, not the nails specifically; the nail infection is tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis.

set1.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What tissue makes up a scale?
opts: Focal loss of epidermis and dermis with destruction of the collagen beneath
Focal loss of epidermis and dermis with collagen destruction is an ulcer; a scale is a compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum.
A compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum, varying in size and thickness
Correct. A scale is a compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum that varies in size and thickness, and psoriasis is an example.
Dried sebum, cellular debris, blood or necrotic skin
Dried sebum, cellular debris, blood or necrotic skin form a crust, as in impetigo; a scale is desquamating stratum corneum.
Thickened epidermis induced by long-term scratching
Epidermal thickening from long-term scratching is lichenification; a scale is a compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum.

set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Where does each step of vitamin D activation take place, beginning in the skin?
opts: Cholecalciferol forms in the skin under ultraviolet B light, then is hydroxylated in the liver and then the kidneys to calcitriol
Correct. The skin only starts the process; two further hydroxylation steps in separate organs are needed before the hormone is active.
Calcitriol is produced directly in the skin under ultraviolet B light and requires no further modification in either the liver or the kidneys at all
The skin produces cholecalciferol, which is inactive until hydroxylated twice elsewhere.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the liver, then hydroxylated in the skin and finally in the kidneys
Production starts in the skin, not the liver: ultraviolet B light forms cholecalciferol, which the liver and then the kidneys hydroxylate.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin and hydroxylated entirely within the kidneys in a single step
Two organs are involved in activation, the liver first and then the kidney.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which structural epidermal changes occur in psoriasis?
opts: Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with fluid accumulating between the two layers of the skin itself
Separation of epidermis from dermis with fluid between them forms a bulla; psoriasis causes epidermal hyperplasia and loss of the stratum granulosum.
Loss of melanocytes from the basal layer
Loss of melanocytes produces the hypopigmentation of vitiligo; psoriasis thickens the epidermis through hyperplasia and loses the stratum granulosum.
Epidermal hyperplasia, loss of the stratum granulosum, and failed lipid secretion causing xeroderma
Correct. Active T cells drive keratinocyte proliferation into epidermal hyperplasia, the stratum granulosum is lost, and epidermal cells stop secreting lipids.
Thinning of the epidermis with slowed keratinocyte division
Thinning with slowed keratinocyte division is atrophy; psoriatic skin cells multiply up to ten times faster, producing epidermal hyperplasia.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: What defines telangiectasia at the tissue level?
opts: Dense inflammatory infiltration around dilated vessels
Inflammatory infiltration is absent in telangiectasia by definition; the vessels are permanently dilated and thinned, not inflamed.
Proliferation of new vessels driven by release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the surrounding dermis over a prolonged period
Vascular endothelial growth factor release with increased capillary density is nail clubbing; telangiectasia is permanent dilatation of superficial dermal vessels.
Permanent dilatation and endothelial thinning of superficial dermal vessels, with NO inflammatory infiltrate
Correct. The dilated, thinned vessels are the capillaries, venules and arterioles of the superficial dermis, and the absence of inflammatory infiltrate is the discriminating feature.
Capillary rupture with blood deposited into the dermis
Capillary rupture depositing blood in the dermis produces petechiae and purpura; telangiectasia is permanent vessel dilatation with no inflammatory infiltrate.

set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What is sebum primarily composed of?
opts: Water, sodium and chloride electrolytes
Water, sodium and chloride make up eccrine sweat; sebum from sebaceous glands is mainly triglycerides, wax esters and squalene.
Keratin and keratohyalin
Keratin comes from keratinocytes and keratohyalin fills the granular layer; sebum is mainly triglycerides, wax esters and squalene.
Collagen and elastin
Collagen and elastin are dermal fibers; sebum is a lipid secretion of triglycerides, wax esters and squalene from sebaceous glands.
Triglycerides, wax esters and squalene
Correct, produced by the sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles to lubricate skin and hair.

set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the site of cellular division?
opts: The granular layer, known as the stratum granulosum
The stratum granulosum holds 3 to 5 layers of diamond-shaped cells with keratohyalin granules; division occurs in the deepest layer, the stratum basale.
The stratum lucidum
The stratum lucidum is 2 to 3 layers of flattened dead keratinocytes, which do not divide; cell division occurs in the stratum basale.
The basal layer, or stratum basale, the deepest layer
Correct. A single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes, which also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.
The stratum corneum, the outermost layer
The stratum corneum is 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes; cell division takes place in the deepest layer, the stratum basale.

set1.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: Which description of collagen in the remodeling phase of wound healing is accurate?
opts: Type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I in small parallel bundles, unlike the basket-weave of normal dermis
Correct. In remodeling, from day 21 to one year, type III collagen gives way to stronger type I in small parallel bundles, unlike the basket-weave of normal dermis.
Type I collagen is replaced with weaker type III collagen oriented in a basket-weave pattern throughout the scar tissue that results
This reverses both: weaker type III is replaced by stronger type I, laid in parallel bundles rather than the basket-weave of normal dermis.
Collagen is degraded entirely and replaced by elastin
Elastin does not replace collagen in a scar; remodeling swaps type III collagen for stronger type I collagen in parallel bundles.
Collagen production continues to increase indefinitely
Production does not rise indefinitely: granulation tissue formation ceases in remodeling while type III collagen is replaced by type I.

set1.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which statement correctly describes androgen regulation of hair?
opts: All three types are equally androgen-dependent
The types differ: terminal hair of the head, beard, axillae and pubic areas is androgen-regulated, while vellus hair grows independently of androgens.
Terminal hair is androgen-regulated; vellus hair grows independently of androgens
Correct. Thick terminal hair on the head, beard, axillae and pubic areas is androgen-regulated; fine vellus hair grows independently of androgens.
Vellus hair is regulated by androgens; terminal hair grows independently of them
This swaps them: vellus hair, the fine short hair of most of the adult body, grows independently of androgens, and terminal hair is androgen-regulated.
Lanugo hair is androgen-regulated; terminal hair is not
Lanugo is the fine hair of newborns, not the androgen-regulated type; terminal hair is the type that androgens regulate.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does human papillomavirus produce a common wart?
opts: It triggers mast cell degranulation in the dermis
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine produces wheals and urticaria; human papillomavirus invades basal cells and drives epidermal proliferation.
It digests keratin using keratinases and proteases
Secreting keratinases and proteases to digest keratin is how dermatophytes metabolize keratin; human papillomavirus instead drives proliferation of the epidermis.
It invades epidermal basal cells via microabrasions, driving epidermal proliferation
Correct. Human papillomavirus invades epidermal basal cells through microabrasions, and that infection leads to proliferation of the epidermis.
It infects the melanocytes that lie along the dermal-epidermal junction within the epidermis
Melanocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction give rise to melanoma; human papillomavirus infects epidermal basal cells through microabrasions.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which description of squamous cell carcinoma is accurate?
opts: Overactivation of the Hedgehog pathway, with pearly papules and telangiectasias
Hedgehog pathway overactivation and pearly papules with telangiectasias describe basal cell carcinoma; squamous cell carcinoma involves tp53 mutation.
Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, with a stuck-on waxy and scaly appearance on the skin
Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 mutation and a stuck-on waxy look describe benign seborrheic keratosis; squamous cell carcinoma shows keratin pearls.
Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and radial growth
Autosomal dominant inherited risk and a radial growth phase belong to melanoma; squamous cell carcinoma involves tp53 mutation and keratin pearls.
Mutation in the tp53 tumor suppressor gene, with keratin pearls and epithelial pearls as pathognomonic features
Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma involves mutation of the tp53 tumor suppressor gene in keratinocytes, and keratin and epithelial pearls are pathognomonic of it.

set1.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Why does psoriatic skin become dry?
opts: The stratum corneum is lost entirely
The stratum corneum is not lost; psoriasis loses the stratum granulosum, and its dryness comes from epidermal cells failing to secrete lipids.
Sebaceous glands overproduce sebum, which dries the surface
Sebum does not dry the skin and is not the psoriasis mechanism; psoriatic dryness, or xeroderma, comes from epidermal cells failing to secrete lipids.
Epidermal cells fail to secrete lipids, producing xeroderma
Correct. In psoriasis, epidermal cells do not secrete lipids, and that failure of secretion produces xeroderma, or dry skin.
Eccrine sweat glands are destroyed by inflammation
Sweat gland destruction plays no part in psoriasis; the dryness, or xeroderma, comes from epidermal cells failing to secrete lipids.

set2.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which receptors carry the sensations of touch and pressure?
opts: Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles
Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles are not skin receptors; touch and pressure are carried by Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells.
Langerhans cells and melanocytes
Langerhans cells are immune sentinels and melanocytes make pigment; touch and pressure are carried by Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells.
Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells
Correct. Meissner's serve fine discriminative touch and low-frequency vibration, Pacinian respond to deep pressure and vibration, and Merkel cells serve light touch.
Ruffini endings, Krause bulbs and free nerve endings only
Free nerve endings sense touch, pain and temperature, but touch and pressure are carried by Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What are the two phases of allergic contact dermatitis?
opts: Irritation, then hyperkeratosis of the stratum corneum
Irritant contact dermatitis needs no prior exposure, and hyperkeratosis is not a phase; allergic contact dermatitis runs through sensitization then elicitation.
Radial growth, then vertical growth
Radial then vertical growth are the growth phases of melanoma; allergic contact dermatitis proceeds through sensitization and then elicitation.
Sensitization, as Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells to form memory; then elicitation, as re-exposure drives T cell migration and inflammation
Correct. Langerhans cells train T cells against a hapten, and re-exposure triggers T cell migration and inflammation, a delayed reaction at 48 to 72 hours.
Sensitization by mast cell degranulation, followed by elicitation through the release of histamine into the surrounding dermal tissue on every subsequent exposure to that same allergen thereafter
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine is the urticaria pathway; allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed, T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which description of the pathology of nail clubbing is accurate?
opts: Incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
Incomplete keratinization at the nail bed produces leukonychia; clubbing shows increased capillary density with vascular endothelial growth factor release.
Increased capillary density, with more vascular endothelial growth factor release
Correct. The main pathologic finding in clubbing is increased capillary density, with increased release of vascular endothelial growth factor.
Overgrowth of the connective tissue within the nail bed itself over a period of time
Connective tissue overgrowth in the nail bed produces Terry's nails; the main pathologic finding in clubbing is increased capillary density.
A halt of keratin production at the matrix
A halt of keratin production causes Beau's lines; clubbing is driven by increased capillary density and vascular endothelial growth factor release.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which mechanism drives psoriasis?
opts: Melanocytes proliferate at the dermal-epidermal junction
Melanocyte proliferation at the dermal-epidermal junction is the origin of melanoma; psoriasis is driven by active T cells infiltrating the epidermis.
Active T cells in the epidermis drive keratinocyte proliferation and excess cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor alpha

Correct. Active T cells infiltrate the epidermis, stimulating keratinocyte proliferation and excess cytokines (tumor necrosis factor alpha, interferon gamma and interleukin-12), so skin cells multiply up to ten times faster.
Mast cells release histamine which drives keratinocyte proliferation
Mast cell histamine release produces the wheals of urticaria; in psoriasis, active T cells stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and excess cytokine production.
Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells, producing a delayed hypersensitivity reaction 48 to 72 hours after each exposure to the allergen in question every single time
Langerhans cells presenting haptens to T cells is allergic contact dermatitis; psoriasis is driven by active T cells and cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which description of seborrheic dermatitis is accurate?
opts: Microbiome dysbiosis, altered immunity and barrier dysfunction, in the sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk
Correct. The cause is incompletely understood, but dysbiosis, altered immunity and barrier dysfunction contribute, in sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk.
A single fungal pathogen acting alone, affecting mainly the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet rather than the sebaceous areas of the skin
No single pathogen explains it, and the palms and soles are not its territory; it affects sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk with several contributing factors.
Autoimmune T cell activation, affecting the elbows and knees
Autoimmune T cell activation on elbows and knees describes psoriasis; seborrheic dermatitis involves dysbiosis, altered immunity and barrier dysfunction.
Ultraviolet damage, affecting sun-exposed skin
Ultraviolet damage to sun-exposed skin underlies actinic keratosis; seborrheic dermatitis favors the sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk.

set2.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: Which description of lichenification is accurate?
opts: Loss of melanocytes across a circumscribed area
Loss of melanocytes produces a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo; lichenification is epidermal thickening from long-term scratching or rubbing.
Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with accumulation of fluid between the two layers, forming a large blister that lifts the surface away
Epidermis separating from dermis with fluid between them forms a bulla; lichenification is hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis from the itch-scratch cycle.
Slowing of keratinocyte division with elastin degradation
Slowed keratinocyte division with elastin degradation is atrophy, which thins the skin; lichenification thickens it through hyperplasia.
Long-term scratching or rubbing in an itch-scratch cycle, causing hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis in thick plaques without scaling
Correct. The itch-scratch cycle drives hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis into firm, thick plaques without scaling, as in lichen simplex chronicus.

set2.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: Which factors cause bullae?
opts: Capillary rupture and thrombocytopenia
Capillary rupture and thrombocytopenia cause petechiae and purpura; bullae arise from mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemicals and autoimmunity.
Androgen stimulation of sebaceous glands
Androgen stimulation is not a cause of blistering; bullae arise from mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemical exposure and autoimmune reactions.
Mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemicals and autoimmunity
Correct, with bullous impetigo as the bacterial example and bullous pemphigoid as the autoimmune one.
Increased melanin production and cumulative ultraviolet light exposure alone
Increased melanin production causes hyperpigmented macules; bullae arise from mechanical, infectious, toxic, chemical or autoimmune injury.

set2.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: A patient has thick, leathery plaques on the neck and forearms with no scaling, after months of scratching. Which secondary lesion is this, mechanistically?
opts: Ulcer, arising from focal loss of both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it
An ulcer is loss of epidermis and dermis, but these plaques are thickened, not eroded; long-term scratching produces lichenification.
Atrophy, from slowed keratinocyte division
Atrophy thins the skin through slowed division and collagen synthesis; thick leathery plaques after scratching reflect lichenification.
Lichenification, from itch-scratch-driven hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis
Correct. The absence of scaling is what separates it from psoriasis, whose plaques do scale.
Scale, from desquamating stratum corneum
Scale is desquamating stratum corneum, and these plaques have none; lichenification forms thick plaques without scaling.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What are the growth phases of melanoma, in order?
opts: Vertical growth down into the dermis first, then radial spread within the epidermis afterwards once the tumor has thickened sufficiently to invade
This reverses the first two: melanoma first multiplies radially within the epidermis, then grows vertically to penetrate the dermis.
Inflammatory, proliferative, then remodeling
Inflammatory, proliferative and remodeling are the phases of wound healing; melanoma progresses radial, vertical, thickening, then metastatic.
Sensitization then elicitation
Sensitization then elicitation are the phases of allergic contact dermatitis; melanoma grows radially, then vertically into the dermis.
Radial growth in the epidermis, vertical growth into the dermis, thickening, then lymphatic and vascular invasion
Correct. Melanoma cells first multiply within the epidermis, then penetrate the dermis, grow deeper and thicker, and finally invade lymphatics and blood vessels.

set2.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: Which description of the proliferative phase of wound healing is accurate?
opts: A fibrin hemostatic plug, over days 1 to 3
A fibrin hemostatic plug forms in the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 3; the proliferative phase, days 4 to 21, forms granulation tissue.
Type I collagen laid down in parallel bundles, over days 21 to one year of remodeling
Type I collagen in parallel bundles belongs to remodeling, day 21 to one year; the proliferative phase forms granulation tissue.
Keratohyalin granules within the granular layer
Keratohyalin granules belong to the normal stratum granulosum; the proliferative phase of wound healing forms granulation tissue over days 4 to 21.
Granulation tissue of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells, days 4 to 21
Correct. Over days 4 to 21, granulation tissue forms, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells, before remodeling begins.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the suspected mechanism of koilonychia?
opts: Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia, leaving a thin, concave nail plate
Correct. Koilonychia is thought to reflect impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia, leaving a weakened, thin, concave nail; the exact pathophysiology is unknown.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal transverse grooves across the surface of the nail plate itself
A halt of keratin production with transverse grooves is Beau's lines; koilonychia is a thin, concave nail from impaired keratin synthesis.
Overgrowth of connective tissue producing an opaque nail
Connective tissue overgrowth with an opaque nail is Terry's nails; koilonychia reflects impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia.
Incomplete keratinization producing white spots
Incomplete keratinization producing white spots is leukonychia; koilonychia is a weakened, concave nail linked to deficiency anemia.

set2.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which layer forms the semi-impermeable barrier of the skin?
opts: The papillary dermis, a thin superficial connective tissue layer
The papillary dermis is a connective tissue layer, not epidermis; the barrier is the stratum corneum of keratin and dead keratinocytes.
The stratum corneum, 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes cemented together
Correct. The stratum corneum, the outermost layer, packs 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes into a semi-impermeable barrier.
The stratum basale, a single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes at the base
The stratum basale is the deepest layer, where cells divide; the barrier is formed by the outermost layer, the stratum corneum.
The stratum granulosum, 3 to 5 layers of diamond-shaped cells
The stratum granulosum holds keratohyalin granules but is not the barrier; the stratum corneum forms the semi-impermeable barrier.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which protein deficiency contributes to atopic dermatitis?
opts: Insufficient collagen, reflecting fibroblast failure
Collagen loss belongs to atrophy and ulceration; atopic dermatitis involves insufficient filaggrin and a compromised epidermal barrier.
Insufficient elastin, reflecting loss of recoil
Elastin degradation is part of atrophy; the protein deficiency in atopic dermatitis is filaggrin, compromising the epidermal barrier.
Insufficient keratohyalin, reflecting loss of the granular layer
Loss of the granular layer is a feature of psoriasis; atopic dermatitis involves insufficient filaggrin from a compromised epidermal barrier.
Insufficient filaggrin, reflecting a compromised epidermal barrier
Correct. Insufficient filaggrin, due to a compromised epidermal barrier, combines with an overactive immune system and genetic, environmental and psychogenic factors.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the mechanism of urticaria?
opts: T cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity 48 to 72 hours after exposure
T cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity is allergic contact dermatitis; urticaria is mast cell degranulation releasing histamine to form wheals.
Dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation from ultraviolet damage
Dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation from ultraviolet damage is actinic keratosis; urticaria results from mast cells releasing histamine.
Capillary rupture with extravasation of blood
Capillary rupture with extravasated blood produces petechiae and purpura; urticaria is histamine-driven wheal formation from mast cells.
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, producing wheals
Correct. In urticaria, mast cells release histamine, which causes vasodilation and plasma leakage into the dermis, forming wheals.

set2.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What gives the spinous layer its alternative name of prickle cell layer?
opts: Keratohyalin granules that give the cells a rough and irregular outline when viewed on microscopy
Keratohyalin granules mark the stratum granulosum above; the spiny look comes from desmosomes connecting the keratinocytes of the spinous layer.
Melanin granules transferred from melanocytes
Melanin transfer does not create the spiny appearance; desmosomes connecting 8 to 10 layers of keratinocytes form the prickle cell layer.
Dead flattened keratinocytes packed into scales
Dead flattened keratinocytes packed into scales form the stratum corneum; the prickle cell appearance comes from desmosomes.
Keratinocytes connected by intercellular connections called desmosomes, which form a spiny appearance
Correct. The 8 to 10 keratinocyte layers of the stratum spinosum are joined by desmosomes, which give the spiny look behind the name prickle cell layer.

set2.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: Which description of an epidermal inclusion cyst is accurate?
opts: A sebaceous gland, and it contains only squalene
An epidermal inclusion cyst does not arise from a sebaceous gland; it arises from a hair follicle and is filled with keratin.
A blood vessel, and it contains clotted blood
Clotted blood is not its content; an epidermal inclusion cyst arises from a hair follicle and contains keratin.
A hair follicle, and it contains keratin
Correct. An epidermal inclusion cyst arises from a hair follicle and contains keratin, enclosed in a capsule within the dermis or subcutaneous layer.
A sweat gland, and it contains sodium and chloride
Eccrine sweat carries sodium and chloride, but an epidermal inclusion cyst arises from a hair follicle and contains keratin.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which description of how dermatophytes infect the skin is accurate?
opts: They proliferate within the dermis, digesting collagen
Dermatophytes do not live in the dermis or digest collagen; they typically occupy the stratum corneum and digest keratin.
Spores secrete keratinases and proteases that digest keratin, typically in the stratum corneum
Correct. Dermatophyte spores secrete keratinases and proteases that digest keratin in skin, hair and nails, and infection typically occurs in the stratum corneum.
They invade epidermal basal cells through microabrasions and drive proliferation of the epidermis above them over time
Invading basal cells through microabrasions is how human papillomavirus causes warts; dermatophytes digest keratin in the stratum corneum.
They release histamine from mast cells producing wheals
Histamine release from mast cells produces urticarial wheals; dermatophyte spores secrete keratinases and proteases to digest keratin.

set2.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: How do eccrine and apocrine sweat glands differ in secretion and function?
opts: Eccrine secrete keratin and apocrine secrete melanin
Neither gland secretes keratin or melanin; eccrine glands secrete water and electrolytes, and apocrine glands secrete protein and fatty lipids.
Eccrine secrete water and electrolytes for evaporative cooling; apocrine, mainly axillary and anogenital, secrete protein and lipids as scent glands
Correct. Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface and cool the body by evaporation; body odor comes from bacterial degradation of apocrine sweat, not from the sweat itself.
Eccrine glands sit in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids; apocrine glands open onto the surface of the skin and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling the body
This swaps the two glands: eccrine glands open onto the skin surface for evaporative cooling, and apocrine glands sit in the axilla and anogenital areas.
Both secrete sebum, differing only in the body regions they occupy
Neither sweat gland secretes sebum; eccrine glands secrete water and electrolytes, apocrine glands protein and fatty lipids, and sebaceous glands make sebum.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which description of the origin of melanoma is accurate?
opts: Within the stratum corneum, transformed by keratinase digestion
Keratinase digestion in the stratum corneum is dermatophyte behavior; melanocytes sit at the dermal-epidermal junction and are damaged by ultraviolet light.
In the reticular layer of the dermis, transformed by dysregulation of the fibroblasts that reside within it over a long period of time
Fibroblast dysregulation drives keloids, not melanoma; melanoma arises from melanocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction after ultraviolet and oxidative damage.
In the basal layer, transformed by Hedgehog pathway activation
Hedgehog pathway activation drives basal cell carcinoma; melanoma arises when ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damage melanocyte DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid).
At the dermal-epidermal junction, with ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damaging melanocyte DNA and leading to uninhibited growth
Correct. Melanoma arises from melanocytes, found at the dermal-epidermal junction, when ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damage their DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid).

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: How is melanoma risk inherited?
opts: As an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance
Correct, though ultraviolet light and oxidative stress remain the primary driving factor.
As an autosomal recessive trait with complete penetrance
Melanoma risk is not recessive with complete penetrance; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance.
As an X-linked trait
Melanoma risk is not X-linked; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance.
It is entirely environmental with no inherited component
Melanoma risk has an inherited component, autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, alongside ultraviolet light and oxidative stress.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: A patient reacts to a nickel earring 48 to 72 hours after wearing it. Which mechanism does the delay reflect?
opts: Viral proliferation within basal keratinocytes
Viral proliferation in basal cells is how human papillomavirus causes warts; the 48 to 72 hour delay reflects T cell-mediated hypersensitivity.
Delayed hypersensitivity: T cells migrate after re-exposure to a hapten once presented by Langerhans cells
Correct. The delay is the time the cellular response takes, which is what distinguishes it from an immediate mast cell reaction.
An immediate immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation occurring upon the very first contact with the metal
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation produces wheals, not a 48 to 72 hour delay; nickel allergy is a delayed T cell-mediated reaction.
Direct chemical injury requiring no prior exposure
Direct chemical injury without prior exposure is irritant contact dermatitis; a 48 to 72 hour delay reflects T cell migration after sensitization.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which description of Beau's lines is accurate?
opts: Increased capillary density, associated with lung disease
Increased capillary density with lung disease describes clubbing; Beau's lines are transverse grooves from a halt of keratin production.
Impaired keratin synthesis, associated with deficiency anemia
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia is koilonychia; Beau's lines come from a halt of keratin production during illness or stress.
A halt of keratin production causing transverse grooves, with illness, stress, nail injury or malnourishment
Correct. Beau's lines are horizontal or transverse grooves caused by a halt of keratin production, associated with illness, stress, nail injury and malnourishment.
Overgrowth of connective tissue within the nail bed, associated with chronic liver disease and with diabetes mellitus in particular
Connective tissue overgrowth in the nail bed is Terry's nails; Beau's lines are grooves from a halt in keratin production.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which skin cancer is the most common malignancy in humans?
opts: Actinic keratosis, which is by far the most common malignancy occurring in human beings
Actinic keratosis is the most common precancer, not a malignancy; basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy in humans.
Basal cell carcinoma, slow growing and rarely metastasizing, typically on the head and neck
Correct. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer and most common human malignancy; it grows slowly and rarely metastasizes.
Squamous cell carcinoma, rapidly metastasizing
Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common skin cancer; basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy in humans.
Melanoma, slow growing and rarely metastasizing
Melanoma is not the most common malignancy, and it can invade lymphatics and blood vessels; basal cell carcinoma holds that place.

set2.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which description of Terry's nails is accurate?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed, associated with aging, liver disease, congestive heart failure or diabetes
Correct. Terry's nails come from overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed, leaving the nail opaque except for a dark band at the tip.
Increased capillary density together with vascular endothelial growth factor release into the tissue locally over time
Increased capillary density with vascular endothelial growth factor release is clubbing; Terry's nails come from connective tissue overgrowth.
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia is koilonychia; Terry's nails reflect overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed produces leukonychia; Terry's nails come from connective tissue overgrowth.

set2.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: Why does an ulcer scar while an erosion generally does not?
opts: An ulcer destroys dermal collagen, which healing must replace; an erosion spares the dermis
Correct. Scarring is a dermal repair process, so a lesion confined above the junction has nothing to scar.
An ulcer is infected and an erosion is sterile
Infection does not define either lesion; the difference is depth, since an ulcer destroys dermal collagen and an erosion stays above the junction.
An ulcer is larger, and size alone determines scarring
Size is not the operative difference; depth is, because an ulcer loses dermis and its collagen while an erosion spares the dermal-epidermal junction.
An ulcer involves a loss of melanocytes from the basal layer which cannot be reversed once it has occurred in the tissue at any point afterwards
Melanocyte loss causes hypopigmentation such as vitiligo; an ulcer is focal loss of epidermis and dermis with destruction of collagen.

set2.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: What is the tissue basis of a papule?
opts: Separation of epidermis from dermis with fluid accumulation
Epidermis separating from dermis with fluid accumulation forms a bulla; a papule is solid, from epidermal hyperplasia and dense dermal collagen.
Focal loss of the epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction beneath it
Focal epidermal loss above the junction is an erosion, a secondary lesion; a papule is an elevated solid lesion from epidermal hyperplasia.
Epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis, over dermal inflammation and dense collagen
Correct. A papule is an elevated solid lesion under 5 millimeters, built from epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis over dermal inflammation, as in seborrheic keratosis.
Fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or beneath the epidermis
Fluid with inflammatory cells within or beneath the epidermis forms a vesicle; a papule is solid, from hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis.

set2.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which statement correctly describes the primary component of the dermis?
opts: Collagen, produced by fibroblasts, providing tensile strength
Correct. Collagen is the primary component of the dermis; fibroblasts produce it, and it provides the skin's tensile strength.
Keratin, produced by keratinocytes, providing an impermeable barrier
Keratin is produced by keratinocytes in the epidermis; the primary dermal component is collagen, made by fibroblasts for tensile strength.
Elastin, produced by mast cells, providing tensile strength
Elastin provides elastic recoil, not tensile strength, and mast cells do not make it; collagen from fibroblasts provides tensile strength.
Melanin, produced by melanocytes, providing ultraviolet protection
Melanin is an epidermal pigment from melanocytes; collagen made by fibroblasts is the primary component of the dermis.

set2.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which statement correctly describes epidermal cell turnover?
opts: Turnover ceases after adolescence
The epidermis keeps turning over, every 30 to 60 days, as cells rise from the basement membrane zone and eventually shed.
Every 30 to 60 days, and turnover is more rapid in younger patients
Correct. Epidermal cells turn over every 30 to 60 days, rising from the basement membrane zone to shed, and turnover is faster in younger patients.
Every 24 to 48 hours, with no age dependence
Every 24 to 48 hours is far too fast; epidermal turnover takes 30 to 60 days and is more rapid in younger patients.
Every 6 to 12 months, and considerably more rapid in older patients
Turnover takes 30 to 60 days, not 6 to 12 months, and it is more rapid in younger patients rather than older ones.

set2.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: How does the mechanism of a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo differ from that of a hyperpigmented macule?
opts: Loss of melanocytes, against increased melanin production in the basal layer of the epidermis
Correct. Vitiligo reflects loss of melanocytes, while hyperpigmented macules such as ephelides, café au lait spots and Mongolian spots reflect increased basal melanin.
Increased melanin production within the epidermis, as against loss of melanocytes entirely
This reverses them: hypopigmentation as in vitiligo is loss of melanocytes, and hyperpigmentation is increased melanin in the basal layer.
Capillary rupture with blood deposition in the dermis
Capillary rupture depositing blood in the dermis produces petechiae and purpura; vitiligo reflects loss of melanocytes.
Dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels
Dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels is telangiectasia; a hypopigmented macule reflects loss of melanocytes.

set2.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: What is the tissue distinction between an erosion and an ulcer?
opts: An erosion stays above the dermal-epidermal junction; an ulcer loses epidermis AND dermis, destroying collagen with inflammatory infiltrate
Correct. The junction is the boundary that separates them, and crossing it is what brings collagen destruction into play.
An erosion involves both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it; an ulcer is limited to the epidermis alone and spares the dermal-epidermal junction entirely, so it never destroys collagen at all
This reverses the two: an erosion stops above the dermal-epidermal junction, while an ulcer loses epidermis and dermis with collagen destruction.
An erosion is fluid-filled and an ulcer is solid
Neither lesion is fluid-filled; an erosion is superficial epidermal loss and an ulcer is loss of epidermis and dermis.
An erosion is a primary lesion and an ulcer is a secondary lesion
Both erosion and ulcer are secondary lesions; they differ in depth, with an ulcer extending through the dermis and destroying collagen.
